title: Advanced Grammar Structures for Sophisticated Expression
objectives: Analyse the function of sophisticated cohesive devices in creating textual unity and argumentative flow
Evaluate the difference between surface cohesion (connectives) and deep coherence (logical and thematic unity) in extended writing
Deploy a range of reference, substitution, ellipsis, and conjunction as cohesive tools in analytical prose
Construct extended analytical writing in which cohesion serves the argument rather than decorating it

authentic_text.title: The Art of the Joined-Up Argument
authentic_text.text:
A well-constructed essay is not simply a collection of accurate observations. What transforms a list of correct points into an argument is coherence — the sense that each idea not only follows from the previous one but is necessary to it. This quality is partly a matter of logic and partly a matter of language, and the two are more intertwined than they might appear.

Linguists distinguish between cohesion — the linguistic means by which a text hangs together on the surface — and coherence — the conceptual unity that makes a text make sense as a whole. A text can be cohesive without being coherent: 'The sky is blue. Furthermore, iron melts at 1,538 degrees Celsius.' The connective 'furthermore' creates an expectation of logical connection that the content does not fulfil. The text is superficially joined but logically disconnected.

Effective academic writing requires both. The connective devices — reference ('this,' 'such an approach,' 'the former'), substitution ('so,' 'do so,' 'the same'), ellipsis (omitting recoverable elements), and conjunction (additive, adversative, causal, and temporal connectives) — are the tools. But tools serve the structure; they do not constitute it. The primary work of making a coherent text is intellectual: ensuring that each claim is genuinely consequential for the next, that each paragraph advances rather than merely continues the argument.

The most common failing in advanced student writing is surface cohesion without conceptual development: a text in which 'however,' 'furthermore,' and 'in addition' appear at regular intervals, but the argument does not actually move. The connectives signal movement; only the ideas can enact it.
authentic_text.source: Adapted from Academic Writing: A University Course Reader, Edinburgh University Press
authentic_text.notes: The article models its own argument: each paragraph follows logically from the previous one and is connected to it both lexically (the repetition of 'cohesion,' 'coherence,' 'argument') and logically (distinguishing the concept, showing its limitation, and specifying its proper application).

critical_reading.question: According to the article, what is the distinction between cohesion and coherence?
critical_reading.answer: Cohesion refers to the linguistic surface features that hold a text together — connectives, reference, substitution, and ellipsis. Coherence refers to the conceptual unity that makes the text make sense as a whole — the logical progression from one idea to the next. A text can be cohesive (linguistically joined) without being coherent (logically unified).

critical_reading.question: What does the writer imply by the example: 'The sky is blue. Furthermore, iron melts at 1,538 degrees Celsius'?
critical_reading.answer: The writer implies that cohesive devices like 'furthermore' create an expectation of logical connection that must be fulfilled by the content — if the content does not follow logically from what precedes it, the connective exposes rather than conceals the gap. The example is deliberately absurd to make the failure of surface cohesion without conceptual coherence vivid.

critical_reading.question: Describe the tone of the final paragraph and identify the rhetorical device used in its last sentence.
critical_reading.answer: The tone is critical and direct — 'the most common failing in advanced student writing is...' names the problem without hedging. The final sentence ('The connectives signal movement; only the ideas can enact it') uses an antithesis — a parallel structure that places two contrasting ideas in formal balance — to make its point memorably. The rhetorical device is antithetical parallelism.

critical_reading.question: The word 'adversative' (paragraph 3) is closest in meaning to:
critical_reading.answer: Expressing contrast or opposition — an adversative connective (such as 'however,' 'nevertheless,' 'on the contrary') signals that what follows stands in contrast or opposition to what precedes it. The term comes from 'adversary' (opponent), reflecting the opposition between the connected ideas.

critical_reading.question: What is the writer's main purpose in this article?
critical_reading.answer: The writer's purpose is to distinguish between surface cohesion and conceptual coherence in academic writing, and to argue that cohesive devices are tools in service of the argument — that the primary work of making a text cohere is intellectual, not linguistic.

language_analysis.explanation:
Cohesive devices are the linguistic tools that create the sense of a text as a connected whole rather than a series of disconnected sentences. The four main categories are: reference (using pronouns, demonstratives, and nominal references to tie one part of the text to another), substitution (using a pro-form to stand in for a previously mentioned item), ellipsis (omitting elements recoverable from context), and conjunction (using logical connectives to signal the relationship between clauses or sentences).

At C1/C2 level, the challenge is to use cohesive devices with precision and restraint — not simply to insert connectives at the beginning of every sentence, but to select the device that most accurately signals the logical relationship intended. 'Furthermore' signals addition; 'moreover' signals addition of something more significant; 'in addition' is more neutral; 'indeed' intensifies or confirms the previous claim. Using them interchangeably is a mark of imprecision.

Sophisticated cohesion also involves reference management: knowing when to use 'this,' 'it,' 'the former,' 'the latter,' 'such an approach,' or a full nominal phrase ('this reliance on surface connectives') to refer back to a previously established concept. The choice between a pronoun and a full nominal reference is not arbitrary — full nominals allow the writer to re-characterise the referent (adding an evaluative element), while pronouns maintain reference without adding new information.

examples.from_text: What transforms a list of correct points into an argument is coherence — the sense that each idea not only follows from the previous one but is necessary to it.
examples.analysis: This sentence uses a wh-cleft for emphasis ('What transforms...is coherence'), then immediately provides a nominal appositive ('the sense that...') to define 'coherence' without requiring a separate defining sentence. The pronoun 'it' in 'necessary to it' refers back to 'previous one' — a pronoun-based cohesive chain that runs across the sentence.

examples.from_text: The connectives signal movement; only the ideas can enact it.
examples.analysis: The pronoun 'it' substitutes for 'movement,' creating a compact elliptical clause. The semicolon rather than a connective performs the contrast — the antithetical structure (connectives vs. ideas, signal vs. enact) creates the opposition without requiring 'however' or 'but,' which would be less elegant.

contrast.formal: The argument proceeds from a distinction that is, in itself, widely accepted. What remains contested, however, is its application to the specific case under examination.
contrast.informal: The basic idea is fine. But using it here is a different matter — that's where the disagreement is.

contrast.formal: This tendency — what might be called the cohesion fallacy — afflicts a significant proportion of advanced student writing across disciplines.
contrast.informal: A lot of students make this mistake: they think adding connectives makes their writing better, but it doesn't if the ideas don't connect.

error_correction.instruction: Each sentence contains one subtle C1/C2 error. Identify and correct it.

sentences.incorrect: The essay's first three paragraphs are well-structured; on the contrary, the fourth lacks the coherent development required to advance the argument.
sentences.correct: The essay's first three paragraphs are well-structured; however, the fourth lacks the coherent development required to advance the argument.
sentences.explanation: 'On the contrary' signals a direct contradiction or denial of the previous claim — it means 'what was just said is wrong.' 'However' signals a contrast or qualification while accepting the previous point. Since the sentence acknowledges the first three paragraphs are good while qualifying the fourth, 'however' is the correct adversative connective.

sentences.incorrect: The article makes a compelling distinction between cohesion and coherence; such a distinction, nevertheless, is rarely applied in practice.
sentences.correct: The article makes a compelling distinction between cohesion and coherence; such a distinction, however, is rarely applied in practice.
sentences.explanation: 'Nevertheless' is a strong concessive adverb used to maintain a main claim in the face of a strong counter-force ('This is difficult; nevertheless, it is necessary'). Here, the writer is simply noting a contrast (the distinction is compelling; it is rarely applied) — 'however' is the more precise choice.

sentences.incorrect: The writers argue that coherence is more fundamental than cohesion, and I agree with their point of view. So does the evidence of their own textual analysis.
sentences.correct: The writers argue that coherence is more fundamental than cohesion, and I agree with their position. So does the evidence of their own textual analysis.
sentences.explanation: 'Point of view' is appropriate for opinions, perspectives, and interpretations. 'Position' is more appropriate in academic writing when referring to an argued intellectual stance — a claim that is presented with evidence and reasoning rather than merely expressed as an opinion.

sentences.incorrect: The most sophisticated academic writers use cohesive devices sparingly, relying instead on the logical structure of their argument to carry the reader through the text.
sentences.correct: The most sophisticated academic writers deploy cohesive devices sparingly, relying instead on the logical structure of their argument to carry the reader through the text.
sentences.explanation: While 'use' is not wrong, 'deploy' is the more precise and idiomatic verb in academic and analytical contexts when describing the deliberate, strategic application of linguistic or rhetorical tools. This is a register refinement appropriate at C2 level.

debate_task.motion: This house believes that explicit instruction in cohesive devices improves academic writing more effectively than instruction in argumentation and critical thinking.
key_arguments: Cohesive devices are specific, teachable, and transferable — students can learn to use them in a single lesson and apply them immediately, generating measurable improvement in text organisation.
For learners writing in a second language, the additional cognitive load of producing content means that explicit linguistic scaffolding (cohesive devices) allows them to concentrate on ideas.

Many academic writing failures are at the surface level — awkward transitions, unclear reference chains — and can be remediated through explicit cohesion instruction without requiring changes to the argument itself.
counter_arguments: The article itself argues that surface cohesion without conceptual development is the most common failing in advanced writing — teaching devices without teaching argument is treating symptoms rather than causes.
Over-reliance on explicit cohesive instruction produces the 'connectives at the start of every sentence' problem identified in the article — a mechanical and superficial form of coherence.

The intellectual work of constructing a genuine argument — identifying implications, anticipating objections, organising evidence — is what makes writing worth reading, and it cannot be substituted by linguistic tools.
discourse_markers: While it is true that... nevertheless,
debate_task.task: Write a 2-minute speech arguing FOR or AGAINST the motion. Use at least 3 discourse markers and one concession.

extended_writing.task: Write an analytical essay responding to the following claim: 'Cohesive devices are the most important feature of effective academic writing.' Your essay should evaluate the claim, drawing on the article's distinction between cohesion and coherence, and arrive at a nuanced position.

structure.guidance: State the claim and signal that you will evaluate rather than simply accept or reject it. Introduce the cohesion/coherence distinction as the framework through which the evaluation will proceed.

Develop the case that cohesive devices genuinely matter — they make the logical structure of an argument visible to the reader, reduce ambiguity, and are associated with the professional register of academic writing. Cite specific examples of cohesive device types (reference, conjunction, ellipsis).

Develop the counter-argument that cohesive devices are necessary but not sufficient — that a text with perfect surface cohesion but weak argumentation will still fail as academic writing. Use the article's example of disconnected but connective-linked sentences.

Resolve the tension by proposing a hierarchy: conceptual coherence (the quality and logic of the argument) is primary; cohesive devices are essential tools in service of that primary goal but cannot substitute for it. Restate the claim's limited truth.

extended_writing.model_answer:
The claim that cohesive devices are the most important feature of academic writing contains a partial truth that, taken in isolation, becomes misleading. Cohesive devices — reference, substitution, ellipsis, and conjunction — are undeniably important. They make an argument's logical structure visible, signal relationships between ideas, and contribute to the professional register that academic writing requires. A text with no connectives, no reference management, and no logical transitions is genuinely difficult to read, regardless of the quality of its ideas.

However, the article makes a distinction that qualifies this importance significantly. Cohesion — the linguistic surface of a text — is not the same as coherence — the conceptual unity that makes the text make sense as a whole. A text in which 'furthermore,' 'however,' and 'in addition' appear at regular intervals is not thereby made coherent. As the article observes, the connectives signal movement; only the ideas can enact it.

Notwithstanding the genuine value of cohesive devices, their over-deployment in the absence of conceptual development is among the most common and identifiable failings in advanced student writing. A paragraph that begins with 'Moreover' must actually add something of significance — the connective creates an obligation the content must fulfil.

The resolution is a hierarchy: coherence is primary; cohesion serves it. The most important feature of effective academic writing is a genuine argument — claims that are consequential for each other, evidence that is genuinely probative, and reasoning that moves rather than repeats. Cohesive devices are the language in which that argument is expressed. They matter because the argument matters; they cannot substitute for it.

advanced_grammar.explanation:
The subjunctive mood in English expresses states or actions that are hypothetical, wished for, demanded, or contrary to fact, rather than actually occurring. It appears in two main forms: the present subjunctive (the base form of the verb: 'It is essential that the argument be clearly structured'), used in formal mandative or concessive constructions; and the past subjunctive ('were,' as in 'If this were a coherent argument'), used in hypothetical conditionals.

The present subjunctive is characteristic of formal written English and appears after verbs of demanding, requiring, recommending, suggesting, and proposing ('The committee recommends that the text be revised'). It is also used in concessive clauses ('Be that as it may,' 'Come what may') and in certain fixed formal expressions ('suffice it to say,' 'as it were'). The past subjunctive ('were') appears in second conditional constructions and signals hypotheticality ('If this claim were well-supported, the argument would succeed').

The communicative purpose of the subjunctive in formal writing is precision: it signals that the writer is discussing something conditional, hypothetical, or mandated rather than actual, and it places the text in the formal register of academic, legal, and policy discourse.
authentic_examples: It is essential that every analytical claim be accompanied by evidence that is both relevant and sufficient.
The article recommends that writers treat cohesive devices as tools in service of the argument rather than as substitutes for it.
Were the text's argument to be as coherent as its surface cohesion, it would represent an exemplary piece of academic writing.

practice.sentence: The examiners require that students support their claims with textual evidence.
practice.transform: Rewrite using the present subjunctive correctly after 'require that.'
practice.answer: The examiners require that students support their claims with textual evidence. (Already correct — 'support' is the subjunctive base form; confirm by checking there is no '-s' on 'support.')

practice.sentence: If the argument was more coherent, the essay would be significantly more persuasive.
practice.transform: Rewrite using the correct subjunctive form 'were' in the conditional.
practice.answer: If the argument were more coherent, the essay would be significantly more persuasive.

practice.sentence: The tutor recommended that the student revises the opening paragraph before submission.
practice.transform: Correct the subjunctive error in this sentence.
practice.answer: The tutor recommended that the student revise the opening paragraph before submission. (The subjunctive base form 'revise' is required after 'recommended that,' not the indicative 'revises.')

quiz.question: According to the article, what is the most common failing in advanced student writing?
options: Insufficient use of cohesive devices and connectives.
Surface cohesion without conceptual development — a text in which connectives are present but the argument does not actually progress.
Overly complex sentence structures that obscure the argument.
Failure to use the academic register consistently throughout the text.
quiz.explanation: The article explicitly identifies 'surface cohesion without conceptual development' as the most common failing — 'a text in which however, furthermore, and in addition appear at regular intervals, but the argument does not actually move.'

quiz.question: What is the function of the phrase 'such an approach' in analytical writing?
options: It is a vague phrase that should be replaced with a specific noun.
It is a nominal reference form that refers back to a previously described approach, allowing the writer to avoid repetition while potentially adding an evaluative characterisation.
It is a discourse marker that signals a transition between two contrasting approaches.
It is a substitute for the first-person 'I,' which is prohibited in academic writing.
quiz.explanation: 'Such an approach' is a demonstrative nominal reference — it refers back to a previously mentioned approach and can add an implicit evaluation ('such a flawed approach,' 'such a promising approach'). This is a more sophisticated reference form than a simple 'it' or 'this approach.'

quiz.question: Identify the error: 'The professor suggested that the student should revise the introduction to improve its coherence.'
options: No error — 'should revise' is grammatically correct after 'suggested that.'
'Should revise' should be 'revise' — the mandative subjunctive after 'suggest that' requires the base form without 'should.'
'Coherence' should be 'cohesion' — the two terms are interchangeable.
'The student' should be preceded by 'her' to clarify reference.
quiz.explanation: After mandative verbs ('suggest,' 'recommend,' 'require,' 'insist') followed by 'that,' formal English uses the subjunctive base form: 'that the student revise,' not 'that the student should revise.' Adding 'should' is common in informal speech but is considered non-standard in formal written English.

quiz.question: Which of the following most accurately uses the distinction between cohesion and coherence?
options: The essay has good coherence — it uses 'however,' 'furthermore,' and 'in addition' throughout.
The essay has good cohesion — its connectives are well-chosen — but lacks coherence, because the claims do not follow from each other logically.
Coherence and cohesion are synonyms that describe the same property of a text.
Coherence refers to sentence-level grammar; cohesion refers to paragraph organisation.
quiz.explanation: Option B correctly uses the distinction: cohesion is the surface linguistic feature (well-chosen connectives), and coherence is the conceptual property (logical progression of claims). Option A confuses the two.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses the past subjunctive 'were' in a formal hypothetical construction?
options: If the argument was clearer, the reader would find it more convincing.
If the argument were clearer, the reader would find it more convincing.
Were the argument to be clear, the reader would have found it more convincing.
If the argument would be clearer, it would be more convincing.
quiz.explanation: Option B correctly uses 'were' (past subjunctive) in the second conditional to signal hypotheticality — the argument is not currently clear. Option A uses 'was' (past indicative), which is acceptable in informal speech but non-standard in formal writing. Option C is a third-person conditional (past hypothetical) which changes the tense and meaning.

listening_exercises.transcript: Advanced grammar is less about new rules than new leverage. Take inversion: 'Never have I seen such results' says what 'I have never seen such results' says, but the fronted negative concentrates emphasis like a spotlight. Cleft sentences redistribute attention: 'What concerns me is the timeline' aims the listener at exactly one constituent. These structures are optional — that is precisely their value. Because you could have said it plainly, choosing the marked form signals deliberateness, and audiences hear the difference even when they cannot name it.
listening_exercises.question: Why does the optionality of these structures matter?
options: Optional rules are easier
Choosing the marked form signals deliberateness
They can be ignored entirely
Examiners prefer plain forms

listening_exercises.transcript: Consider three refinements that mark sophisticated prose. Participle clauses compress: 'Having reviewed the data, the committee revised its estimate' folds two sentences into one flowing period. Nominalization abstracts: 'they decided quickly' becomes 'the speed of their decision' — useful for topic management, dangerous in bulk, since heavily nominalized prose loses agents and energy. And subjunctive survivals — 'I suggest that he be informed,' 'were I in your position' — persist precisely in formal registers, where their rarity makes them legible as care.
listening_exercises.question: What is the danger of heavy nominalization?
options: It is ungrammatical
Prose loses agents and energy
It shortens sentences too much
It sounds too casual
